articles.title: Bob Mackie obituary
articles.summary: American fashion designer and costumier who clothed glamorous showbiz celebrities, especially Cher. Most costume designers are novelists, supplying character, back stories, social placement and history, done in cloth.
body: Mackie, who has died aged 87, was master of the showbiz sartorial aesthetic that evolved on stage and in films to entertain in itself as well as project performers.

Rhinestones, sequins, beads, plaques, plumes, plush, le tout ensemble. An audience got a big kick from a Mackie costume before a word was spoken or a note was sung, and performers had total confidence in him, as he studied their bodies, movements and personality before designing.
He did that with divas from Judy Garland through Diana Ross, Barbra Streisand, Bette Midler, Whitney Houston, Madonna and, especially, Cher.

Theirs was an interactive relationship from Cher’s television appearances in the 70s, when he guided her out of hippiedom and into minimal material spectacularly styled. He and she plotted the crest of black feathers she wore to the 1986 Academy Awards, atop an outfit that linked back to the extreme exoticism of early movie stars such as Gloria Swanson. What little there was of it was perfectly executed; Mackie costumes were made to couture standards – even his reworkings of second-hand gowns for a broke Tina Turner.
points: American fashion designer and costumier who clothed glamorous showbiz celebrities, especially Cher.

articles.title: I love my life and my cup is full but I’m drowning in shame for things left undone. How can I balance it all? | Leading questions
articles.summary: You are not the only one, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. It will help to ask whether you have a time problem or a bandwidth problem. I love my life in so many ways.
body: I love my life in so many ways. I have a rewarding job, I’m making stellar progress towards a graduate degree, I have incredible friends and community, plus I’m even reconnecting with estranged family. My cup is very full but I still feel grief and shame for how much falls to the wayside.

I have missed countless doctors’ appointments. My vehicle’s license plates have been expired for almost a year. I often apologise to angry friends and acquaintances after they confront me for not seeing them in months. My significant other says she doesn’t see me enough. So do my parents. I clock out of work and shudder at the thought of facing my growing avalanche of text messages. I panic whenever I receive an email that demands I arrange yet another appointment or submit to a lengthy phone call. The stack of forms I’m overdue to submit makes me feel so irresponsible, as if I’m the only adult alive who can’t seem to take care of business.
points: You are not the only one, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes.
It will help to ask whether you have a time problem or a bandwidth problem.

articles.title: Toxic bosses: why do companies protect managers who make working life hell?
articles.summary: Bullying, manipulation and intimidation can destroy lives, yet abusive authoritarians continue to rise to the top. How do they get away with it – and can they be brought to heel? When Andrea finally resigned, her colleagues told her the truth they had always known about her boss. Some apologised.
body: Andrea was a senior legal executive with decades of credibility when she began reporting to a powerful new colleague. Within months, something was wrong. Expectations shifted without warning and feedback contradicted itself. He spoke over her in public and undermined her in private. Slowly she began questioning not just him but herself, her competence, even her grip on reality.

What disturbed Andrea most was the gradual discovery that everybody already knew. Colleagues confessed that when they heard this executive was returning to the organisation, they had cried. When Andrea approached HR, a senior executive told her: “People work longer at McDonald’s than they work for him.” That was acknowledgment, not discovery. And there is something brutally revealing in the stab-vest description. Andrea had become the organisation’s psychological shock absorber. While she took the blows, everybody around her was safer.
points: Bullying, manipulation and intimidation can destroy lives, yet abusive authoritarians continue to rise to the top.
How do they get away with it – and can they be brought to heel?

articles.title: ‘Going places with panache’: Max Mara channels audacious women for Milan show
articles.summary: Chore jackets and loose-fit trousers nod to ‘nonconformist glamour’ of Amelia Earhart and other pioneers. The Max Mara catwalk at Milan fashion week had well-cut coats, sturdy block-heeled boots, crisp white shirts and capacious suede handbags.
body: Trousers were pleated and roomy, skirts long enough to be elegant but not long enough to trip you up. In shades of sand and chalk, grey and black, every piece was designed to work with everything else, and to blend into an existing wardrobe. The styling gestures – a popped collar here, a knotted belt there – stopped short of gimmick. The models could have walked off the runway and on to the Milan street – which, Griffiths said backstage, was the point. “The catwalk show is only the prelude to what to me is the real presentation, which is when I see women walking down the street in my clothes.”

Recently, even this most adult and sensible of brands has sometimes been unable to resist the temptation to chase the youth vote. This season, Max Mara went back to doing what it does best, which is fashion for grownups. (Nothing here for wearing in da club.) Griffiths said: “We were founded on the simple mantra of real clothes for real women, back in the 1960s, and when we stick to that idea, we never go wrong. So more than ever, I wanted to focus on real life chic.”

articles.title: Why Chefs Love Cooking on Stainless Steel
articles.summary: Stainless steel cookware is experiencing a cultural renaissance. This isn’t to say that the genre of cookware ever disappeared, but, once upon a lockdown, it felt like an ad from a nonstick cookware brand was always a scroll away.
body: If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

So, why is virtually every commercial kitchen stocked with stainless steel cookware? Eater spoke with Carlye Lester, the sous chef at HAGS, a queer fine dining restaurant in New York City, about why she loves to reach for it at her restaurant, and so many other chefs and cooks do at theirs. The main benefit? Reliability. “I love that it gets super hot and heats evenly; it is [easy] to get a good sear on whatever you are making,” Lester says, explaining that she’s using stainless steel pans to sear and crisp a mustard marinaded-cod at HAGS. “[And] I love that stainless steel can be more reliable than a nonstick if you’re using the correct methods.”

That’s one of the greatest misconceptions about stainless steel cookware: that it is not nonstick. In actuality, if you heat up stainless steel cookware to the right temperature (around 400 degrees Fahrenheit, or once a few water droplets in the pan start beading instead of evaporating), and add a bit of oil, it creates a nonstick effect due to something called the Leidenfrost effect.

articles.title: Post-Marni, Francesco Risso Forges a New Creative Practice With the Bureau of Imagination
articles.summary: Within a 1920s factory in Milan, Francesco Risso and Alex Sossah are building a home, an atelier, and an ever-evolving laboratory for clothes, objects, art, and ideas.
body: “I was born on a boat. I learned to walk barefoot on wood, in the sway, imbalanced. Even today I sway on parallel bars to see the sky upside down. My dad had a carriage, my mum a tailor shop; together an armoured ship of dreams, some cumbersome, some powerful, some very dangerous.”

After 10 years at Prada and almost a decade transforming Marni into one of fashion’s most distinctive brands, Risso has recently taken on the creative direction of GU, Uniqlo’s sister brand, while simultaneously opening the Bureau, which he calls “a manufacturing house for objects.”

While the building that houses the Bureau was originally intended to be their home, not long after Risso and Sossah settled in, the space began to transform into something else. Risso has never been particularly interested in separating life from work, or work from imagination, and by now those boundaries have all but disappeared. He might wake up and paint, work on a garment, cook, welcome a friend, or find someone already making something in another room. “The Bureau has become less my house and more a house for imagination,” he says. “I happen to sleep in it.”

articles.title: Lili Reinhart Breaks Down Her Rom-Com References for ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Press Tour
articles.summary: “It started with a Pinterest board called ‘Rom-Com Baddie’ that I made and shared with my stylist, Ib Abdel Nasser,” Lili Reinhart tells Vogue.
body: Like many a modern press tour, Lili Reinhart’s globe-spanning, Y2K-ified endeavor to promote her new film, The Love Hypothesis, began on Pinterest.

Reinhart and Nasser originally planned to stick to the poppy colors and flirty silhouettes of the era. “The board slowly evolved from general references into photos of characters from those films and their iconic looks, and that’s really where the idea of doing various homages came from,” she explains. In pivoting to specific movie looks, the pair also had the chance to flex their vintage fashion muscles—including a one-of-a-kind Elie Saab couture gown from spring 2004.

Co-curator Judith Clark shares her perspective on the convergence between Surrealism and fashion as art forms through the lens of the new exhibition.

The Palazzo Reale exhibition unfolds along a single thread: chronologically. articles.title: These Are the 5 Luckiest Zodiac Signs of Libra Season
articles.summary: With the “back to school” energy of Virgo season behind us, it’s time to get the Libra party started. But which star signs will be the luckiest among the mix?
body: Virgo season has been a lovely, down-to-earth period, with plenty of us basking in that “back to school” energy. That said, having spent some time getting our lives in order, it can leave us feeling a little shy when it comes to connecting with others, or uncertain about where we fit in.

But Libra season? This period—which kicks off from September 22 until October 23—is, much like the sign itself, both stylish and sociable. Think: cocktail soirées, the tail end of fashion month parties, and making new friends and acquaintances. It’s also a very lucky period for a handful of zodiac signs. And by “lucky,” we mean filled with new opportunities, connections, and plenty of adventure.
